sources.note: Contributed the AI-tell catalog. Filtered from 37 patterns to the ~21 that fire in a technical register and compressed to one-line rows.
Contributed the composition rules. Strunk's 18 rules condensed to the 8 that apply to short technical prose. The elements-of-style reference files were dropped.

modifications: Authoring-first, not editing-first: humanizer's draft/audit/final rewrite loop, travel-blog example, DETECTION GUIDANCE, and PERSONALITY AND SOUL sections were dropped.
Scope narrowed to repo and forge prose. Voiced and long-form prose stays with humanizer.
Dropped curly-quote pattern (Claude emits straight ASCII) and the Wikipedia-article framing of the significance, notability, and challenges patterns.

Added a content rule (carry why, not what), length-and-silence rules, git-shaped worked examples, guidance for error messages, log lines, and code comments, and anti-patterns specific to agent-written git prose. None of these exist upstream.
Inverted upstream's diff-anchored-writing rule for commits, changelogs, and migration guides, where narrating the change is correct.
DO NOT TOUCH condensed to five lines and extended to identifiers, CLI flags, and file paths.
Renamed from repo-prose to oss-writing on migration into oss-kit.
Split into a core and one reference file. The tell catalog moved to references/tells.md and loads only when a draft is suspect, per R-SKL-07; the core keeps a single link to it.

Added four composition rules paraphrased from ASD-STE100 Issue 9 (name the referent, cap noun stacks at three, one instruction per step, keep the articles), and its sentence, paragraph, and noun-stack figures as limits: under 20 words in an instruction, under 25 in an explanation, under six sentences in a paragraph. They were stated as signals to split rather than limits until a skill change measured that a signal does not bind. ASD-STE100 is copyright ASD and an EU registered trademark. No rule text, dictionary entry, or other wording was copied from it; the rules were written from its principles and it is cited by name. Its approved-word dictionary and no-gerund rule were rejected as a poor fit for software prose. Its rule against omitting a verb, subject, or article to shorten text is why the keep-the-articles rule survives a pass aimed at brevity.
Added a normative statements section for the RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 uppercase keywords.

Attached a reason to every hard constraint and moved the worked examples into <example> tags, following Anthropic's Claude 5 context engineering post, the Opus 5 prompting page, and the prompting best practices page.

Added a nominalized gerund chain row to the catalog. Prefer-the-common-word folded into the AI-vocabulary row and synonym drift into elegant variation, because both already existed there under other names.
Dropped the duplicate commit-body example and shortened the bad half of each remaining pair.

Replaced the per-artifact content table for commits and change requests with one length ladder: the body defaults to none and exists only on one of six named triggers. The table listed what a body carries and read as a checklist to cover. A template's required sections still win over the ladder, which decides how much each one gets rather than whether it appears.

Split the GitHub and GitLab render mechanics into references/forge-rendering.md, loaded only at the branch that needs it, per R-SKL-07. The body keeps one forge-agnostic wrapping rule. Nothing upstream has this content.

Replaced the bad-and-good example pairs for git prose with finished artifacts at each rung, each named for the trigger that earned its body. The bad halves demonstrated the padded output the skill was still producing, so the recognition half was not working. Pairs stay in references/tells.md, where the contrast is the lesson.
Narrowed the ban on working-process narration to the author's route to the fix. Naming the failure a change targets is a reproduction, which Git's SubmittingPatches requires of a commit body.
